name: Elimination diet

card.summary: Temporarily removing suspected trigger foods, then reintroducing them one at a time; established for diagnosing food allergy and eosinophilic esophagitis, with little trial evidence for finding skin triggers.
card.note: Strict versions can cause nutrient gaps and are generally done with dietitian guidance; people with a history of severe reactions need medical supervision.

quick.overview:
An elimination diet removes suspected foods for a period (roughly two weeks to two months in Wikipedia's description), tracks symptoms, then reintroduces foods one at a time to see whether symptoms return. It is mainly a diagnostic procedure for food allergy and food intolerance.

In looksmaxxing communities it appears as a way to find foods that worsen acne or skin. Medical evidence for elimination diets is strongest in gut conditions such as eosinophilic esophagitis; studies of skin triggers via this method are not in the research reviewed here.
quick.mechanism: Foods suspected of causing reactions are cut out, a symptom and food diary is kept, and foods are challenged back in sequence. For allergic or intolerance conditions this tests whether a specific food drives symptoms.
quick.risks: Wikipedia notes the diet must be nutritionally complete, symptoms may briefly worsen at the start, and strict versions are generally not recommended in pregnancy. People with asthma, laryngeal oedema or a history of anaphylaxis may need testing where resuscitation is available. Unvalidated tests such as Vega machine testing have not been shown to be effective.

lead: An elimination diet, also called an exclusion or oligoantigenic diet, is a diagnostic procedure for identifying foods that cause adverse effects, whether from food allergy, food intolerance or other causes. A suspected food is removed for about two weeks to two months while symptoms are monitored, and foods are then reintroduced one at a time [1].

It is used mainly to diagnose food allergy and chemical food intolerance and occasionally as a treatment diet [1]. Its best-documented clinical role is in conditions such as eosinophilic esophagitis, where six-food elimination diets have been studied in children and adults [2][3][4][5].

In looksmaxxing communities it is mentioned as a way of finding foods that trigger acne or other skin changes. The studies reviewed here concern gut and allergic conditions; no clinical studies of elimination diets for appearance or acne outcomes were found.

paras: Patients remove suspected foods, keep records of food, medication and symptoms, and then reintroduce foods one by one. Wikipedia says challenges should begin only after symptoms have cleared and after at least two weeks on the diet, and that dietitian guidance is strongly recommended [1].

Common targets include dairy, wheat, eggs, soy, nuts, fish and shellfish; the six-food version used in eosinophilic esophagitis research removes the most common allergens together [2][3][6]. Grokipedia describes symptom diaries and a hypoallergenic base diet, and a 2 to 6 week elimination phase [7].

Wikipedia credits Albert Rowe with proposing the concept in 1926 and describing it in his 1941 book on elimination diets and allergies. In 1978 Australian researchers Gibson and Clancy published an exclusion diet to identify dietary chemical triggers in chronic idiopathic urticaria [1].
Research on elimination diets is concentrated on gastrointestinal and allergic disease rather than skin appearance.

In eosinophilic esophagitis, a retrospective study of a six-food elimination diet in children reported clinical and histologic responses [3]. A study in 50 adults assessed a six-food elimination diet followed by reintroduction to identify causative foods and reported histologic response, symptoms and quality of life outcomes [4]. A systematic review and meta-analysis examined dietary interventions for histologic remission [5]. Other studies used skin prick and patch tests to direct food elimination [8][9], and a prospective study examined an empiric six-food diet in adults [10].

A 2001 review addressed gluten elimination in coeliac disease, where gluten removal leads to mucosal recovery in genetically susceptible people [11]. A study in dogs with chronic enteropathies used an elimination diet trial and is veterinary research, not human [12].
No clinical studies of elimination diets for acne or other cosmetic skin outcomes were found in this research.

Wikipedia notes symptoms may worsen briefly at the start, the diet needs to be nutritionally complete, and strict forms are generally not recommended during pregnancy; people with a history of severe reactions may need supervised testing [1]. Grokipedia also notes the risk of lower calcium, iron or fibre intake if the diet is prolonged without guidance [7].

Wikipedia reports that the field of food allergy and intolerance has long lacked universal definitions and diagnostic standards, and that Vega machine testing has not been shown to be effective [1]. Skin prick and blood tests can help identify immediate allergic reactions but can yield false positives [1].

Elimination approaches are discussed in skin-focused communities as a way to test personal triggers such as dairy or sugar. Wikipedia's acne article states that the evidence for dairy and acne is weak and observational and that lower-glycaemic-load diets are better supported [13].

timeline.event: Albert Rowe proposes the elimination diet concept [1].
Rowe describes elimination diets in a book on allergies [1].
Gibson and Clancy publish an exclusion diet for chronic idiopathic urticaria triggers [1].
Study of six-food elimination in adults with eosinophilic esophagitis [4].

lore.intro: Elimination diets are discussed in appearance communities as a route to personal skin triggers, usually alongside dairy and sugar removal.

claims.claim: Removing trigger foods can reveal and clear personal acne or skin triggers
claims.believers: Proponents say removing common irritants such as dairy and then reintroducing them shows which foods affect their skin.
claims.experts: Wikipedia's acne article describes the evidence on dairy and acne as weak and observational and says milk restriction lacked sufficient evidence as of 2014 [13]. No clinical studies of elimination diets for acne were found.

claims.claim: Elimination diets identify food allergies and intolerances
claims.believers: Advocates describe them as a standard way to find triggers when tests are inconclusive.
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes the exclusion-then-challenge method as used to confirm food allergy and intolerance, with skin and blood tests prone to false positives [1]; eosinophilic esophagitis studies support its use in that condition [3][4][5].
